quoted_phrases: What I got instead was a set of organising instincts—patterns the Loomio founders have learned the hard way while building software for groups that don’t rely on hierarchy to get things done.
The throughline was simple: decentralisation doesn’t happen by default.
It’s designed, practised, and maintained.
Below are the eight patterns as they were taught, with what landed for me in the room and how we’ve started to apply them.
Intentionally produce counter-culture (“belonging is a superpower”) The facilitators were explicit: if you want a decentralised group, you have to create a culture that makes it possible.
That means designing for belonging—rituals, language, onboarding, and signals that say “you’re allowed to act here”.
What we took away is that “culture” isn’t a backdrop.
It’s an active system.
If you don’t build it, the default culture (often hierarchical, often exclusionary) fills the gap.
Systematically distribute care labour (stewards and stewardees) Care work—checking in, following up, smoothing conflict—keeps groups alive, but it’s usually invisible and unevenly carried.
Naming that out loud shifted the conversation from “people should step up” to “the system needs to change”.
Make explicit norms and boundaries “Unwritten rules are just rules some people don’t know yet.” That line stuck.
The facilitators pushed us to externalise norms—how decisions are made, how conflict is handled, what’s in scope and what isn’t.
What felt “obvious” internally wasn’t obvious at all.
Keep talking about power Decentralisation doesn’t eliminate power; it redistributes it.
The answers weren’t always aligned with formal roles.
Even compressed, it produced a more considered outcome than a typical “any objections?” moment.
Agree how you use tech (the “holy trinity”: realtime / async / static) Most groups accumulate tools without agreement.
The “holy trinity” frames three modes: 	•	Realtime (e.g.
Use rhythm to cut information overload Information overload isn’t just volume; it’s unpredictability.
It created “edges” around work, which is what people need to manage attention.
Generate new patterns together The final pattern is meta: don’t just adopt patterns—create them.
After introducing the patterns, the facilitators had us adapt them to our contexts, then share back what we’d changed.
What mattered wasn’t fidelity to the original model, but the act of collective design.
That’s what builds ownership and keeps the system adaptable.
⸻ What changed for us The workshop didn’t give us a finished operating model.
We’ve started pairing stewards and stewardees, with a simple expectation of regular check-ins.
We’re moving proposals into an async space with clear timelines, and documenting outcomes in a static location.
We’ve drafted a short set of working agreements and put them somewhere everyone can find (and edit).
•	We’re naming power earlier.
•	We’re testing a rhythm.
That’s the point.
•	Power doesn’t disappear.
The facilitators didn’t present these as problems to solve once.
They’re conditions to manage continuously.
You don’t get it by hiring the right people or declaring flatness.
“Belonging is a superpower” sounded soft at first.
That’s the loop these patterns are trying to sustain.
